title: Heaps & Intervals
scopeHtml: Scope: top-K with a heap, running median with two heaps, k-way merge, merging intervals, meeting rooms.

notes.title: Heaps and top-K
notes.html:
Idea. A heap (priority queue) always gives you the smallest (min-heap) or largest (max-heap) element in O(1) and lets you insert or remove it in O(log n). It is the right tool when you repeatedly need "the best remaining item" without fully sorting.

Recognise it when: "k-th largest", "top K frequent", "merge K sorted", "schedule by priority", "running median".

Heap tools by language (know the default direction!):

Default Max-heap via
C++ priority_queue max-heap priority_queue<int, vector<int>, greater<int>> for min
Java PriorityQueue min-heap Collections.reverseOrder() or a comparator
Kotlin PriorityQueue min-heap compareByDescending { }
Python heapq min-heap push negated values

Worked example: Top K Frequent Elements. Count frequencies, then keep a min-heap of size k: the smallest of the current top k sits on top and is evicted when something more frequent arrives. This is O(n log k), better than sorting all n items.

Languages: C++ · Java · Kotlin · Python
vector<int> topKFrequent(vector<int>& nums, int k) {
    unordered_map<int, int> cnt;
    for (int x : nums) cnt[x]++;
    using P = pair<int, int>;                                  // (frequency, value)
    priority_queue<P, vector<P>, greater<P>> pq;               // min-heap
    for (auto& [v, c] : cnt) {
        pq.push({c, v});
        if ((int)pq.size() > k) pq.pop();                      // drop the least frequent
    }
    vector<int> out;
    while (!pq.empty()) { out.push_back(pq.top().second); pq.pop(); }
    return out;
}
int[] topKFrequent(int[] nums, int k) {
    Map<Integer, Integer> cnt = new HashMap<>();
    for (int x : nums) cnt.merge(x, 1, Integer::sum);
    PriorityQueue<int[]> pq = new PriorityQueue<>((a, b) -> a[0] - b[0]);   // min-heap by freq
    for (var e : cnt.entrySet()) {
        pq.offer(new int[]{e.getValue(), e.getKey()});
        if (pq.size() > k) pq.poll();                                       // drop the least frequent
    }
    int[] out = new int[k];
    for (int i = 0; i < k; i++) out[i] = pq.poll()[1];
    return out;
}
fun topKFrequent(nums: IntArray, k: Int): IntArray {
    val cnt = nums.groupingBy { it }.eachCount()
    val pq = java.util.PriorityQueue<Map.Entry<Int, Int>>(compareBy { it.value })   // min-heap
    for (e in cnt.entries) {
        pq.offer(e)
        if (pq.size > k) pq.poll()                                                  // drop the least frequent
    }
    return pq.map { it.key }.toIntArray()
}
import heapq
from collections import Counter

def top_k_frequent(nums, k):
    cnt = Counter(nums)
    heap = []                                       # min-heap of (frequency, value)
    for v, c in cnt.items():
        heapq.heappush(heap, (c, v))
        if len(heap) > k:
            heapq.heappop(heap)                     # drop the least frequent
    return [v for c, v in heap]
    # shortcut: [v for v, _ in cnt.most_common(k)]

Complexity. O(n log k) time, O(n) space for the counts. Bucket sort by frequency gives O(n).

Why a min-heap for "top K largest"? The heap root is the k-th largest so far, the one to evict next. A max-heap of all n items would cost O(n log n).

Industry examples. Trending hashtags and top-K dashboards, OS task schedulers, Dijkstra's algorithm, event simulators, and merge steps in external sorting and database engines.

Everyday analogy. A podium with k places: a new athlete only matters if they beat the current slowest podium finisher, who then steps down.

Common interview traps.

  • Using the wrong heap direction (max vs min) and returning the smallest K.
  • Sorting everything when only the top K is required.
  • Mutable tie-breaking: tuples compare element by element in Python and C++ pairs; define the order you intend.

notes.title: Two heaps and the running median
notes.html:
Idea. Keep the lower half of the numbers in a max-heap and the upper half in a min-heap, sized so that the median is at one or both tops. Insert in O(log n), read the median in O(1).

Worked example: Find Median from Data Stream.

Invariants: every element in lo ≤ every element in hi, and len(lo) is either equal to len(hi) or one larger.

Languages: C++ · Java · Kotlin · Python
class MedianFinder {
    priority_queue<int> lo;                                   // max-heap (lower half)
    priority_queue<int, vector<int>, greater<int>> hi;        // min-heap (upper half)
public:
    void addNum(int x) {
        lo.push(x);
        hi.push(lo.top()); lo.pop();                          // balance: largest of lower goes up
        if (hi.size() > lo.size()) { lo.push(hi.top()); hi.pop(); }
    }
    double findMedian() {
        return lo.size() > hi.size() ? lo.top() : (lo.top() + hi.top()) / 2.0;
    }
};
class MedianFinder {
    PriorityQueue<Integer> lo = new PriorityQueue<>(Collections.reverseOrder());  // lower half
    PriorityQueue<Integer> hi = new PriorityQueue<>();                             // upper half
    void addNum(int x) {
        lo.offer(x);
        hi.offer(lo.poll());                                  // largest of lower goes up
        if (hi.size() > lo.size()) lo.offer(hi.poll());
    }
    double findMedian() {
        return lo.size() > hi.size() ? lo.peek() : (lo.peek() + hi.peek()) / 2.0;
    }
}
class MedianFinder {
    private val lo = java.util.PriorityQueue<Int>(compareByDescending { it })   // lower half
    private val hi = java.util.PriorityQueue<Int>()                             // upper half
    fun addNum(x: Int) {
        lo.offer(x)
        hi.offer(lo.poll())                                   // largest of lower goes up
        if (hi.size > lo.size) lo.offer(hi.poll())
    }
    fun findMedian(): Double =
        if (lo.size > hi.size) lo.peek().toDouble() else (lo.peek() + hi.peek()) / 2.0
}
import heapq

class MedianFinder:
    def __init__(self):
        self.lo = []        # max-heap via negation (lower half)
        self.hi = []        # min-heap (upper half)

    def add_num(self, x):
        heapq.heappush(self.lo, -x)
        heapq.heappush(self.hi, -heapq.heappop(self.lo))     # largest of lower goes up
        if len(self.hi) > len(self.lo):
            heapq.heappush(self.lo, -heapq.heappop(self.hi))

    def find_median(self):
        if len(self.lo) > len(self.hi):
            return float(-self.lo[0])
        return (-self.lo[0] + self.hi[0]) / 2

Complexity. addNum O(log n), findMedian O(1), space O(n).

Industry examples. Latency percentile estimates in monitoring (exact for small windows, approximated by t-digest or HDR histograms at scale), and moving-median filters in sensor data.

Everyday analogy. Two queues on either side of a median line: when one grows too long, move its end person across.

Common interview traps.

  • Forgetting the rebalance step, so sizes drift and the median is wrong.
  • Using integer division for the average of two middles.
  • Python has no max-heap; negate values carefully.

notes.title: K-way merge
notes.html:
Idea. To merge k sorted sequences, keep a min-heap of the current head of each sequence. Pop the smallest, output it, and push the next element from the same sequence. Time O(N log k) for N total elements.

Worked example: Merge K Sorted Lists (linked lists). The heap holds one node per list.

Languages: C++ · Java · Kotlin · Python
ListNode* mergeKLists(vector<ListNode*>& lists) {
    auto cmp = [](ListNode* a, ListNode* b) { return a->val > b->val; };     // min-heap
    priority_queue<ListNode*, vector<ListNode*>, decltype(cmp)> pq(cmp);
    for (auto* l : lists) if (l) pq.push(l);
    ListNode dummy(0), *tail = &dummy;
    while (!pq.empty()) {
        ListNode* n = pq.top(); pq.pop();
        tail->next = n; tail = n;
        if (n->next) pq.push(n->next);
    }
    return dummy.next;
}
ListNode mergeKLists(ListNode[] lists) {
    PriorityQueue<ListNode> pq = new PriorityQueue<>((a, b) -> a.val - b.val);   // min-heap
    for (ListNode l : lists) if (l != null) pq.offer(l);
    ListNode dummy = new ListNode(0), tail = dummy;
    while (!pq.isEmpty()) {
        ListNode n = pq.poll();
        tail.next = n; tail = n;
        if (n.next != null) pq.offer(n.next);
    }
    return dummy.next;
}
fun mergeKLists(lists: Array<ListNode?>): ListNode? {
    val pq = java.util.PriorityQueue<ListNode>(compareBy { it.`val` })           // min-heap
    lists.filterNotNull().forEach { pq.offer(it) }
    val dummy = ListNode(0)
    var tail = dummy
    while (pq.isNotEmpty()) {
        val n = pq.poll()
        tail.next = n; tail = n
        n.next?.let { pq.offer(it) }
    }
    return dummy.next
}
import heapq

def merge_k_lists(lists):
    heap = [(l.val, i, l) for i, l in enumerate(lists) if l]   # index breaks ties (nodes are not comparable)
    heapq.heapify(heap)
    dummy = tail = ListNode()
    while heap:
        _, i, node = heapq.heappop(heap)
        tail.next = node
        tail = node
        if node.next:
            heapq.heappush(heap, (node.next.val, i, node.next))
    return dummy.next

Complexity. O(N log k) time, O(k) extra space. Divide and conquer (merge pairs repeatedly) achieves the same time.

Industry examples. External merge sort for data larger than memory, merging sorted log files or LSM-tree SSTables (RocksDB, Cassandra compaction), and merging search results from shards.

Everyday analogy. Several checkout lines each with sorted tickets: look at the front ticket of every line and serve the smallest.

Common interview traps.

  • Python tie comparison error: when values tie, the heap compares the nodes; add a tiebreaker index.
  • Pushing whole lists instead of one head per list.

notes.title: Intervals: sort, then sweep
notes.html:
Idea. Most interval problems become easy after sorting by start time and walking once, keeping the "current" merged interval.

Worked example: Merge Intervals.

Languages: C++ · Java · Kotlin · Python
vector<vector<int>> mergeIntervals(vector<vector<int>>& iv) {
    sort(iv.begin(), iv.end());                                     // by start
    vector<vector<int>> out;
    for (auto& cur : iv) {
        if (out.empty() || out.back()[1] < cur[0]) out.push_back(cur);   // gap: new interval
        else out.back()[1] = max(out.back()[1], cur[1]);                  // overlap: extend
    }
    return out;
}
int[][] mergeIntervals(int[][] iv) {
    Arrays.sort(iv, (a, b) -> Integer.compare(a[0], b[0]));       // by start
    List<int[]> out = new ArrayList<>();
    for (int[] cur : iv) {
        if (out.isEmpty() || out.get(out.size() - 1)[1] < cur[0]) out.add(cur);   // gap
        else out.get(out.size() - 1)[1] = Math.max(out.get(out.size() - 1)[1], cur[1]);  // overlap
    }
    return out.toArray(new int[0][]);
}
fun mergeIntervals(iv: Array<IntArray>): List<IntArray> {
    val out = mutableListOf<IntArray>()
    for (cur in iv.sortedBy { it[0] }) {                          // by start
        if (out.isEmpty() || out.last()[1] < cur[0]) out.add(cur.copyOf())     // gap
        else out.last()[1] = maxOf(out.last()[1], cur[1])                      // overlap
    }
    return out
}
def merge_intervals(iv):
    iv.sort()                                                    # by start
    out = []
    for s, e in iv:
        if not out or out[-1][1] < s:
            out.append([s, e])                                   # gap: new interval
        else:
            out[-1][1] = max(out[-1][1], e)                      # overlap: extend
    return out

Complexity. O(n log n) for sorting, O(n) for the sweep.

Touching intervals. [1,2] and [2,3] overlap if endpoints are inclusive; decide the rule with the interviewer (use < vs <=).

Industry examples. Calendar free/busy merging, merging IP ranges and firewall rules, and coalescing disk or memory allocations.

Everyday analogy. Combining overlapping bookings of a hall into continuous blocks.

Common interview traps.

  • Not sorting first.
  • Updating the end with cur[1] instead of max(end, cur[1]) when one interval contains another.
  • Mutating the input intervals when a copy is expected.

notes.title: Meeting rooms: counting overlaps
notes.html:
Idea. The minimum number of rooms equals the maximum number of simultaneous meetings. Sort the start times and end times separately and sweep with two pointers, or sort by start and use a min-heap of end times.

Worked example: Meeting Rooms II (heap version): the heap contains the end times of rooms currently in use. If the earliest ending meeting finishes before the new one starts, reuse that room.

Languages: C++ · Java · Kotlin · Python
int minMeetingRooms(vector<vector<int>>& m) {
    sort(m.begin(), m.end());
    priority_queue<int, vector<int>, greater<int>> ends;         // end times of busy rooms
    for (auto& v : m) {
        if (!ends.empty() && ends.top() <= v[0]) ends.pop();     // reuse the freed room
        ends.push(v[1]);
    }
    return ends.size();
}
int minMeetingRooms(int[][] m) {
    Arrays.sort(m, (a, b) -> a[0] - b[0]);
    PriorityQueue<Integer> ends = new PriorityQueue<>();         // end times of busy rooms
    for (int[] v : m) {
        if (!ends.isEmpty() && ends.peek() <= v[0]) ends.poll(); // reuse the freed room
        ends.offer(v[1]);
    }
    return ends.size();
}
fun minMeetingRooms(m: Array<IntArray>): Int {
    val ends = java.util.PriorityQueue<Int>()                    // end times of busy rooms
    for (v in m.sortedBy { it[0] }) {
        if (ends.isNotEmpty() && ends.peek() <= v[0]) ends.poll()   // reuse the freed room
        ends.offer(v[1])
    }
    return ends.size
}
import heapq

def min_meeting_rooms(m):
    m.sort()
    ends = []                                                    # end times of busy rooms
    for s, e in m:
        if ends and ends[0] <= s:
            heapq.heappop(ends)                                  # reuse the freed room
        heapq.heappush(ends, e)
    return len(ends)

Complexity. O(n log n) time, O(n) space.

Industry examples. Conference room schedulers, CPU/core assignment, and cloud capacity "peak concurrency" counts.

Everyday analogy. A restaurant seating plan: a table is reused as soon as the previous party leaves.

Common interview traps.

  • Comparing < vs <= for meetings that end exactly when another starts.
  • Forgetting to sort by start time.

notes.title: Summary
notes.html: A heap gives the best remaining item in O(log n): use a size-k min-heap for top-K (O(n log k)), two heaps (max-heap for the lower half, min-heap for the upper half) for a running median, and a heap of heads for k-way merge in O(N log k). Know each language's default heap direction. For intervals, sort by start and sweep, extending the current interval with max of ends; the minimum number of rooms is the maximum number of simultaneous intervals, computed with a min-heap of end times.

questions.promptHtml: Return the k most frequent elements of an array. Why a min-heap of size k, and what is the complexity?

sections.label: Why interviewers ask this
sections.html: Tests heap direction intuition and trading sort for a bounded heap.

sections.label: 30-second answer
sections.html: Count frequencies with a hash map, then keep a min-heap of size k keyed by frequency. Push each entry and pop the smallest when the size exceeds k, so the heap always holds the k most frequent seen so far. O(n log k) time, O(n) space. Bucket sort by frequency gives O(n).

sections.label: Deep explanation
sections.html:
For the top k largest, the item to evict is the smallest of the current k, which is the root of a min-heap. A max-heap of everything would be O(n log n). Mind each language's default direction.

Languages: C++ · Java · Kotlin · Python
vector<int> topKFrequent(vector<int>& nums, int k) {
    unordered_map<int, int> cnt;
    for (int x : nums) cnt[x]++;
    using P = pair<int, int>;
    priority_queue<P, vector<P>, greater<P>> pq;
    for (auto& [v, c] : cnt) {
        pq.push({c, v});
        if ((int)pq.size() > k) pq.pop();
    }
    vector<int> out;
    while (!pq.empty()) { out.push_back(pq.top().second); pq.pop(); }
    return out;
}
int[] topKFrequent(int[] nums, int k) {
    Map<Integer, Integer> cnt = new HashMap<>();
    for (int x : nums) cnt.merge(x, 1, Integer::sum);
    PriorityQueue<int[]> pq = new PriorityQueue<>((a, b) -> a[0] - b[0]);
    for (var e : cnt.entrySet()) {
        pq.offer(new int[]{e.getValue(), e.getKey()});
        if (pq.size() > k) pq.poll();
    }
    int[] out = new int[k];
    for (int i = 0; i < k; i++) out[i] = pq.poll()[1];
    return out;
}
fun topKFrequent(nums: IntArray, k: Int): IntArray {
    val cnt = nums.groupingBy { it }.eachCount()
    val pq = java.util.PriorityQueue<Map.Entry<Int, Int>>(compareBy { it.value })
    for (e in cnt.entries) {
        pq.offer(e)
        if (pq.size > k) pq.poll()
    }
    return pq.map { it.key }.toIntArray()
}
import heapq
from collections import Counter

def top_k_frequent(nums, k):
    heap = []
    for v, c in Counter(nums).items():
        heapq.heappush(heap, (c, v))
        if len(heap) > k:
            heapq.heappop(heap)
    return [v for c, v in heap]

sections.label: Common mistakes & traps
sections.html:
• Using a max-heap and returning the wrong end.
  • Sorting everything for O(n log n).

sections.label: Follow-ups
sections.html:
1. Kth largest in an array? → Min-heap of size k; the root is the answer (or Quickselect, O(n) average).
  2. Streaming data? → Maintain the size-k heap incrementally.
  3. When is bucket sort better? → Frequencies are bounded by n, so O(n).

sections.label: 3-YOE vs senior answer
sections.html: Senior mentions Quickselect, bucket sort and tie handling.

questions.promptHtml: Design a structure supporting addNum and findMedian over a data stream. What are the invariants?

sections.label: Why interviewers ask this
sections.html: A well-known hard-ish design with heaps.

sections.label: 30-second answer
sections.html: Keep the lower half in a max-heap and the upper half in a min-heap. Invariants: every element of the lower half is ≤ every element of the upper half, and the lower heap has the same size or one more element. Add in O(log n), read the median from the tops in O(1).

sections.label: Deep explanation
sections.html:
On insert, push into the lower heap, move its top to the upper heap, then rebalance if the upper heap got larger. The median is the lower top (odd count) or the average of both tops (even count).

Languages: C++ · Java · Kotlin · Python
class MedianFinder {
    priority_queue<int> lo;
    priority_queue<int, vector<int>, greater<int>> hi;
public:
    void addNum(int x) {
        lo.push(x);
        hi.push(lo.top()); lo.pop();
        if (hi.size() > lo.size()) { lo.push(hi.top()); hi.pop(); }
    }
    double findMedian() {
        return lo.size() > hi.size() ? lo.top() : (lo.top() + hi.top()) / 2.0;
    }
};
class MedianFinder {
    PriorityQueue<Integer> lo = new PriorityQueue<>(Collections.reverseOrder());
    PriorityQueue<Integer> hi = new PriorityQueue<>();
    void addNum(int x) {
        lo.offer(x);
        hi.offer(lo.poll());
        if (hi.size() > lo.size()) lo.offer(hi.poll());
    }
    double findMedian() {
        return lo.size() > hi.size() ? lo.peek() : (lo.peek() + hi.peek()) / 2.0;
    }
}
class MedianFinder {
    private val lo = java.util.PriorityQueue<Int>(compareByDescending { it })
    private val hi = java.util.PriorityQueue<Int>()
    fun addNum(x: Int) {
        lo.offer(x)
        hi.offer(lo.poll())
        if (hi.size > lo.size) lo.offer(hi.poll())
    }
    fun findMedian(): Double =
        if (lo.size > hi.size) lo.peek().toDouble() else (lo.peek() + hi.peek()) / 2.0
}
import heapq

class MedianFinder:
    def __init__(self):
        self.lo, self.hi = [], []          # lo is a max-heap via negation

    def add_num(self, x):
        heapq.heappush(self.lo, -x)
        heapq.heappush(self.hi, -heapq.heappop(self.lo))
        if len(self.hi) > len(self.lo):
            heapq.heappush(self.lo, -heapq.heappop(self.hi))

    def find_median(self):
        if len(self.lo) > len(self.hi):
            return float(-self.lo[0])
        return (-self.lo[0] + self.hi[0]) / 2

sections.label: Common mistakes & traps
sections.html:
• Skipping the rebalance step.
  • Integer division when averaging two middle values.

sections.label: Follow-ups
sections.html:
1. Sliding window median? → Two heaps with lazy deletion, or an order-statistic tree.
  2. Values in a small range [0, 100]? → A counting array and walk to the median.
  3. Billions of values? → Approximate with t-digest or histograms.

sections.label: 3-YOE vs senior answer
sections.html: Senior discusses approximations for scale (t-digest) and lazy deletion.

questions.promptHtml: Merge k sorted linked lists. Compare heap and divide-and-conquer approaches.

sections.label: Why interviewers ask this
sections.html: The k-way merge pattern appears in databases and external sorting.

sections.label: 30-second answer
sections.html: Put the head of each list in a min-heap, repeatedly pop the smallest, append it to the result, and push its successor. That is O(N log k) for N total nodes. Divide and conquer, merging lists pairwise, has the same complexity and O(1) extra heap space beyond recursion.

sections.label: Deep explanation
sections.html:
The heap never holds more than k nodes. In Python add an index tie-breaker because nodes are not comparable. A dummy head avoids special-casing the first node.

Languages: C++ · Java · Kotlin · Python
ListNode* mergeKLists(vector<ListNode*>& lists) {
    auto cmp = [](ListNode* a, ListNode* b) { return a->val > b->val; };
    priority_queue<ListNode*, vector<ListNode*>, decltype(cmp)> pq(cmp);
    for (auto* l : lists) if (l) pq.push(l);
    ListNode dummy(0), *tail = &dummy;
    while (!pq.empty()) {
        ListNode* n = pq.top(); pq.pop();
        tail->next = n; tail = n;
        if (n->next) pq.push(n->next);
    }
    return dummy.next;
}
ListNode mergeKLists(ListNode[] lists) {
    PriorityQueue<ListNode> pq = new PriorityQueue<>((a, b) -> a.val - b.val);
    for (ListNode l : lists) if (l != null) pq.offer(l);
    ListNode dummy = new ListNode(0), tail = dummy;
    while (!pq.isEmpty()) {
        ListNode n = pq.poll();
        tail.next = n; tail = n;
        if (n.next != null) pq.offer(n.next);
    }
    return dummy.next;
}
fun mergeKLists(lists: Array<ListNode?>): ListNode? {
    val pq = java.util.PriorityQueue<ListNode>(compareBy { it.`val` })
    lists.filterNotNull().forEach { pq.offer(it) }
    val dummy = ListNode(0)
    var tail = dummy
    while (pq.isNotEmpty()) {
        val n = pq.poll()
        tail.next = n; tail = n
        n.next?.let { pq.offer(it) }
    }
    return dummy.next
}
import heapq

def merge_k_lists(lists):
    heap = [(l.val, i, l) for i, l in enumerate(lists) if l]
    heapq.heapify(heap)
    dummy = tail = ListNode()
    while heap:
        _, i, node = heapq.heappop(heap)
        tail.next = node
        tail = node
        if node.next:
            heapq.heappush(heap, (node.next.val, i, node.next))
    return dummy.next

sections.label: Common mistakes & traps
sections.html:
• Python comparing nodes on ties (add an index).
  • Pushing all nodes instead of one head per list.

sections.label: Follow-ups
sections.html:
1. Where else is it used? → External merge sort, LSM-tree compaction, merging shard results.
  2. Complexity if lists have lengths n1..nk? → O(N log k) with N = sum.
  3. Smallest range covering k lists? → Same heap plus tracking the current maximum.

sections.label: 3-YOE vs senior answer
sections.html: Senior connects it to real systems like compaction and shard merging.

questions.promptHtml: Merge overlapping intervals. What is the key step and the common bug?

sections.label: Why interviewers ask this
sections.html: Checks sort-then-sweep thinking and boundary details.

sections.label: 30-second answer
sections.html: Sort by start time, then walk once keeping the last merged interval: if the next interval starts after its end, start a new one; otherwise extend the end to the maximum of both ends. O(n log n) time.

sections.label: Deep explanation
sections.html:
Sorting guarantees that any overlap is with the most recent merged interval. The max handles the case where one interval fully contains the next. Decide with the interviewer whether touching endpoints ([1,2], [2,3]) merge.

Languages: C++ · Java · Kotlin · Python
vector<vector<int>> mergeIntervals(vector<vector<int>>& iv) {
    sort(iv.begin(), iv.end());
    vector<vector<int>> out;
    for (auto& cur : iv) {
        if (out.empty() || out.back()[1] < cur[0]) out.push_back(cur);
        else out.back()[1] = max(out.back()[1], cur[1]);
    }
    return out;
}
int[][] mergeIntervals(int[][] iv) {
    Arrays.sort(iv, (a, b) -> Integer.compare(a[0], b[0]));
    List<int[]> out = new ArrayList<>();
    for (int[] cur : iv) {
        if (out.isEmpty() || out.get(out.size() - 1)[1] < cur[0]) out.add(cur);
        else out.get(out.size() - 1)[1] = Math.max(out.get(out.size() - 1)[1], cur[1]);
    }
    return out.toArray(new int[0][]);
}
fun mergeIntervals(iv: Array<IntArray>): List<IntArray> {
    val out = mutableListOf<IntArray>()
    for (cur in iv.sortedBy { it[0] }) {
        if (out.isEmpty() || out.last()[1] < cur[0]) out.add(cur.copyOf())
        else out.last()[1] = maxOf(out.last()[1], cur[1])
    }
    return out
}
def merge_intervals(iv):
    iv.sort()
    out = []
    for s, e in iv:
        if not out or out[-1][1] < s:
            out.append([s, e])
        else:
            out[-1][1] = max(out[-1][1], e)
    return out

sections.label: Common mistakes & traps
sections.html:
• Forgetting to sort.
  • Setting the end to cur[1] instead of max(end, cur[1]).

sections.label: Follow-ups
sections.html:
1. Insert an interval into a sorted list? → Add before, merge overlaps, add after in O(n).
  2. Remove the minimum intervals to make the rest non-overlapping? → Greedy by earliest end.
  3. Can a person attend all meetings? → Sort and check adjacent overlap.

sections.label: 3-YOE vs senior answer
sections.html: Senior clarifies endpoint semantics up front and mentions the greedy relatives.

questions.promptHtml: Find the minimum number of meeting rooms needed. Explain the heap approach and the sweep alternative.

sections.label: Why interviewers ask this
sections.html: Shows you can translate "rooms" into "maximum overlap".

sections.label: 30-second answer
sections.html: The answer is the maximum number of meetings happening at the same time. Sort by start time and keep a min-heap of end times of rooms in use: if the earliest ending meeting finishes by the new start, reuse that room; otherwise add one. The heap size at the end is the answer. O(n log n).

sections.label: Deep explanation
sections.html:
The sweep alternative sorts starts and ends separately and walks two pointers, incrementing a counter on each start and decrementing on each end; the peak counter value is the answer.

Languages: C++ · Java · Kotlin · Python
int minMeetingRooms(vector<vector<int>>& m) {
    sort(m.begin(), m.end());
    priority_queue<int, vector<int>, greater<int>> ends;
    for (auto& v : m) {
        if (!ends.empty() && ends.top() <= v[0]) ends.pop();
        ends.push(v[1]);
    }
    return ends.size();
}
int minMeetingRooms(int[][] m) {
    Arrays.sort(m, (a, b) -> a[0] - b[0]);
    PriorityQueue<Integer> ends = new PriorityQueue<>();
    for (int[] v : m) {
        if (!ends.isEmpty() && ends.peek() <= v[0]) ends.poll();
        ends.offer(v[1]);
    }
    return ends.size();
}
fun minMeetingRooms(m: Array<IntArray>): Int {
    val ends = java.util.PriorityQueue<Int>()
    for (v in m.sortedBy { it[0] }) {
        if (ends.isNotEmpty() && ends.peek() <= v[0]) ends.poll()
        ends.offer(v[1])
    }
    return ends.size
}
import heapq

def min_meeting_rooms(m):
    m.sort()
    ends = []
    for s, e in m:
        if ends and ends[0] <= s:
            heapq.heappop(ends)
        heapq.heappush(ends, e)
    return len(ends)

sections.label: Common mistakes & traps
sections.html:
• Wrong < vs <= for back-to-back meetings.
  • Not sorting by start time.

sections.label: Follow-ups
sections.html:
1. Return the room assignment, not just the count? → Heap of (end, room id).
  2. Streaming meetings? → A balanced tree or sorted structure.
  3. Weighted intervals? → DP.

sections.label: 3-YOE vs senior answer
sections.html: Senior gives both the heap and the sweep and states the equivalence to maximum overlap.

questions.contextHtml: A trending-searches feature computes the top 10 queries over the last hour from a stream of 50,000 events per second spread across 40 servers. The current version streams every event to one machine that sorts a map of counts every minute, and that machine now runs out of memory and misses its deadline.
questions.promptHtml: How would you redesign it so it scales 10x?

sections.label: What a weak answer looks like
sections.html: Buys a bigger machine and keeps sorting the whole map.

sections.label: Strong answer
sections.html:
1. Clarifying questions I'd ask: Exact or approximate top-K acceptable? Cardinality of queries? Freshness requirement? Window sliding or tumbling?
  2. Immediate mitigation: Pre-aggregate counts per server per minute so only counts, not raw events, travel.
  3. Hypotheses, ranked: One node aggregates all raw events; sorting the full map is O(n log n); memory grows with the number of distinct queries.
  4. How I'd verify: Measure distinct-query cardinality and memory per node.
  5. Root cause: No partial aggregation and no bounded structure.
  6. Fix: Each server keeps counts for the current minute and sends a compact summary. Partition by query hash so each aggregator owns a key range and keeps a size-k min-heap; a final step merges the per-partition top-10 heaps (k-way merge of small lists). For a sliding hour, keep per-minute buckets and subtract expired minutes. If cardinality is huge, use a Count-Min Sketch plus a heap of heavy hitters (approximate).
  7. Prevention: Load test with realistic skew; set memory caps and alarms.
  8. Trade-offs: Exactness versus memory: sketches are bounded but approximate; partitioning avoids a single hot node but needs a merge step.

sections.label: Curveball follow-ups
sections.html:
• A viral query dominates one partition? → Split hot keys or use local pre-aggregation and a two-stage merge.
  • Late-arriving events? → Allow a small lateness window or reconcile periodically.

sections.label: Senior war story
sections.html: Moving to per-partition heaps and a final top-K merge cut the aggregator's memory by 95% and the compute time from minutes to seconds.

sections.label: Scoring rubric
sections.html:
• No hire: bigger machine, sort everything.
  • Hire: partial aggregation, heap of size k, merge.
  • Strong hire: partitioning, sliding buckets, sketches and skew handling.
